slides.0.title: The CMS deductive tasting format
slides.0.subtitle: In limited time, move from evidence to grape, region and vintage
slides.1.title: The deductive flow
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Sight and nose
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Sight: clarity, brightness, colour and rim variation; nose: fruit type and condition (fresh, ripe, jammy, dried), non-fruit (floral, herbal, spice), earth or mineral, and the presence and type of oak
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Palate
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Confirm the nose, then judge sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body and finish; structure is the most reliable basis for narrowing down
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Initial and final conclusions
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Initial conclusion: Old or New World, cool or warm climate, possible varieties, age range; final conclusion: grape, country, region, appellation and vintage
slides.1.content: Deduction is about elimination: every observation should shorten the list of candidates.
slides.2.title: Key decision points and exam formats
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Old World and New World
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Common tendencies: the Old World shows more earth, mineral and non-fruit notes with restrained fruit and higher acidity; the New World riper fruit, higher alcohol and often more obvious oak. Tendencies, not laws, and warming is blurring the line
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Judging oak
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Oak or not, new or old, and type: American oak leans to coconut, dill and vanilla, French oak to toast, spice and fine tannins; oak use often points straight at region and price tier
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Exam formats by level
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Taking the Americas chapter as an example: Certified is 4 wines (2 red, 2 white), written, in 45 minutes; Advanced and Master are commonly described as 6 wines in about 25 minutes, spoken aloud. Rules differ by chapter, so check official information before entering
slides.2.content: Spoken CMS tasting rewards speed and rhythm: a fixed order of description matters more than flowery adjectives.
slides.3.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What does the final conclusion in CMS deductive tasting usually require?
A. Grape, country, region, appellation and vintage
D. Only whether it tastes good
The initial conclusion covers Old/New World, climate and age range.
Coconut and dill notes most often point to which oak?
French oak leans to toast and spice.
Short answer: describe the common clues for “Old World vs New World” and the limits of this judgement.
Old World: more earth, mineral and non-fruit notes
Old World: restrained fruit, higher acidity
New World: riper fruit, higher alcohol, more obvious oak
Limit: these are tendencies, not laws
Limit: warming and shifting winemaking styles blur the line

Old World wines often show more earth, mineral and non-fruit notes, restrained fruit and higher acidity; New World wines often show riper fruit, higher alcohol and more obvious oak. But these are only tendencies: warming makes European wines riper, and many New World producers now pick earlier with less oak, so treat it as a starting point for narrowing down, then confirm with structural evidence.
